I am a 44-year-old woman farmer in Quzhou County, and my family has about 10 mu of good flat land. I went to middle school, and I have been making the farming decisions for our household for over 20 years. In our village, the land is irrigated from wells, and the standard practice is double-cropping — wheat followed by maize — because we have to make full use of the growing season.

My wheat is already in the ground; we sowed it last October after rotary-tilling the fields. Right now, at the start of spring, I am focused on managing that wheat — it needs one more irrigation and a urea topdressing before it heads in May. I will harvest it in early June, and immediately after cutting it, I will plant summer maize using no-tillage direct seeding. That saves me time and diesel, and the hybrid maize varieties like Denghai or Zhongke give much better yields.

I also keep 2 mu for cotton. I am planting it now in late March and early April. Cotton is labor-intensive — I have to spray pesticides more than ten times for bollworm and aphids — but it brings in cash, which we need for daily expenses. I do not plant more than 2 mu because our family labor is limited; my husband and I handle most of the work, and the wheat-maize system is our food security base.

For fertilizer, I rely mainly on compound fertilizer as a basal dressing for all three crops, and I topdress the wheat with urea in spring. We irrigate from the village well: the wheat gets winter irrigation plus three more times in spring; the maize gets two or three times in summer; and the cotton gets two or three times depending on the rainfall.
